question_html: Under section 139(1), who may be appointed as auditor of a company, and at which meeting must every company make such appointment?

options.A: Every company shall appoint an individual or a firm (which includes a Limited Liability Partnership incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008) as an auditor of the company at its first Annual General Meeting; the term 'appointment' includes re-appointment
options.B: Every company shall appoint only an individual (and never a firm or LLP) as its auditor, and such appointment must be made at the first Board meeting held after incorporation rather than at any general meeting
options.C: Every company shall appoint an individual or a body corporate (other than a firm or LLP) as its auditor, and such appointment must be made at an extraordinary general meeting convened specifically for that purpose
options.D: Every company shall appoint an individual or a firm as its auditor, but such appointment must be made at the second Annual General Meeting, since the first AGM is reserved exclusively for adoption of financial statements

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Every company shall appoint an individual or a firm (which includes a Limited Liability Partnership incorporated under the LLP Act, 2008) as an auditor of the company at its first Annual General Meeting; the term 'appointment' includes re-appointment

Section 139(1) permits appointment of either an individual or a firm (including an LLP) as auditor, and the appointment (a term that includes re-appointment) must be made at the company's first Annual General Meeting, holding office thereafter as prescribed by the section.

question_html: Where a company is required to constitute an Audit Committee under section 177 and the Board agrees with the Committee's recommended auditor, what is the next procedural step, and what happens if the Board instead disagrees?

options.A: If the Board agrees, it must independently re-verify the auditor's eligibility before placing the matter before members; if it disagrees, it may unilaterally recommend a different auditor to members without referring the matter back to the Audit Committee at all
options.B: If the Board agrees with the Audit Committee's recommendation, it shall further recommend the individual or firm as auditor to the members in the AGM for appointment; if the Board disagrees, it shall refer the recommendation back to the Committee for reconsideration, citing reasons for the disagreement
options.C: The Board's agreement or disagreement is legally irrelevant, since under Rule 3 the Audit Committee's recommendation is final and binding and must be placed before members verbatim, with the Board having no power to refer it back
options.D: If the Board agrees, the matter must be referred to the Registrar of Companies for approval before being placed before members; if it disagrees, the matter is automatically escalated to the Tribunal for a final decision

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) If the Board agrees with the Audit Committee's recommendation, it shall further recommend the individual or firm as auditor to the members in the AGM for appointment; if the Board disagrees, it shall refer the recommendation back to the Committee for reconsideration, citing reasons for the disagreement

Rule 3 provides that where the Board agrees with the Audit Committee's recommendation, it shall further recommend that individual or firm to the members in the AGM; where it disagrees, it shall refer the recommendation back to the Committee for reconsideration citing reasons - and if the Committee, after considering those reasons, declines to reconsider, the Board records its own reasons for disagreement and sends its own recommendation to members.

question_html: Under section 177 read with the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, which classes of company are required to constitute an Audit Committee (relevant as the 'competent authority' for auditor selection under Rule 3), and what relief is available if a company later ceases to meet the applicable thresholds?

options.A: Only listed public companies are required to constitute an Audit Committee; unlisted public companies are entirely exempt from this requirement regardless of their paid-up capital, turnover, or borrowings
options.B: Every public company (listed or unlisted) is required to constitute an Audit Committee irrespective of size, and once constituted the requirement can never lapse even if the company's paid-up capital, turnover, and borrowings all subsequently fall to nil
options.C: Every listed public company, and every other public company having paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, or turnover of Rs. 100 crore or more, or aggregate outstanding loans/borrowings/debentures/deposits exceeding Rs. 50 crore, must constitute an Audit Committee; a company that ceases to fulfil any of these three conditions for three consecutive years is relieved of the requirement until it again meets any of them
options.D: Every private company having paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more is required to constitute an Audit Committee, while public companies are exempt from this requirement under section 177

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Every listed public company, and every other public company having paid-up capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, or turnover of Rs. 100 crore or more, or aggregate outstanding loans/borrowings/debentures/deposits exceeding Rs. 50 crore, must constitute an Audit Committee; a company that ceases to fulfil any of these three conditions for three consecutive years is relieved of the requirement until it again meets any of them

Section 177 read with the relevant Rules requires an Audit Committee for every listed public company and for other public companies crossing any one of the paid-up capital (Rs. 10 crore), turnover (Rs. 100 crore), or aggregate borrowings (Rs. 50 crore) thresholds (assessed as on the date of the last audited financial statements); ceasing to meet all three conditions for three consecutive years relieves the company of the requirement until any condition is met again.

question_html: Before an auditor's appointment is made, what two things must be obtained from the proposed auditor, and what four matters must the certificate specifically confirm?

options.A: Only an oral confirmation of willingness from the proposed auditor is required, and no written certificate is mandated under Rule 4 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014
options.B: The written consent alone suffices under Rule 4; the certificate confirming eligibility, compliance with statutory terms and limits, and disclosure of pending proceedings is required only for auditors of listed companies, not unlisted companies
options.C: A certificate is required stating only that the auditor has adequate professional indemnity insurance; no written consent to the appointment, and no certification regarding eligibility, statutory terms, limits, or pending proceedings, is required under Rule 4
options.D: The written consent of the auditor to the appointment, and a certificate confirming: (a) eligibility for appointment and no disqualification under the Companies Act, the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, or rules thereunder; (b) that the proposed appointment is as per the terms provided under the Act; (c) that the proposed appointment is within the limits laid down by or under the authority of the Act; and (d) that the list of pending proceedings against the auditor, firm, or any partner regarding professional matters of conduct, as disclosed in the certificate, is true and correct

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The written consent of the auditor to the appointment, and a certificate confirming: (a) eligibility for appointment and no disqualification under the Companies Act, the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, or rules thereunder; (b) that the proposed appointment is as per the terms provided under the Act; (c) that the proposed appointment is within the limits laid down by or under the authority of the Act; and (d) that the list of pending proceedings against the auditor, firm, or any partner regarding professional matters of conduct, as disclosed in the certificate, is true and correct

Rule 4 read with section 139(1) mandates that before appointment, the auditor's written consent must be obtained, along with a certificate covering all four specified matters - eligibility/no disqualification, compliance with the Act's terms, compliance with prescribed limits, and the truth and correctness of any disclosed pending professional-conduct proceedings; the certificate must also indicate whether the section 141 criteria are satisfied.

question_html: Within what period must a company file notice of an auditor's appointment with the Registrar, and in what form and time-frame must certain body corporates governed by the NFRA Rules, 2018 intimate NFRA of an auditor's appointment under section 139(1)?

options.A: The company shall inform the auditor of the appointment and file a notice in Form ADT-1 with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed; separately, under Rule 3(3) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, every body corporate (other than a 'company' as defined in section 2(20)) governed under the NFRA Rules shall, within 15 days of appointment of an auditor under section 139(1), inform NFRA in Form NFRA-1 of the particulars of the auditor appointed
options.B: The company must file Form ADT-3 with the Registrar within 30 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed, and no separate intimation to NFRA is required under any circumstance
options.C: The company must file Form ADT-1 with the Registrar within 60 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed, and NFRA-governed body corporates must intimate NFRA in Form NFRA-2 within 60 days of appointment
options.D: The company must file Form ADT-2 with the Registrar within 15 days of the date of registration of the company (not the date of the appointing meeting), and no separate NFRA intimation obligation exists for body corporates governed under the NFRA Rules

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The company shall inform the auditor of the appointment and file a notice in Form ADT-1 with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed; separately, under Rule 3(3) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, every body corporate (other than a 'company' as defined in section 2(20)) governed under the NFRA Rules shall, within 15 days of appointment of an auditor under section 139(1), inform NFRA in Form NFRA-1 of the particulars of the auditor appointed

Form ADT-1 must be filed with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting at which the auditor is appointed; separately and additionally, NFRA-governed body corporates (other than companies as defined in section 2(20)) must, per Rule 3(3) of the NFRA Rules, 2018, intimate NFRA in Form NFRA-1 within 15 days of appointment of an auditor under section 139(1) - a distinct filing from the one-time Rule 3(2) intimation due within 30 days of commencement of the NFRA Rules for existing auditors.

question_html: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the certificate to be obtained from a proposed auditor under Rule 4 from the notice to be filed with the Registrar under section 139(1)?

options.A: Both the certificate and the Registrar notice are one and the same document, filed jointly by the auditor and the company with the Registrar within 30 days of the date of registration of the company
options.B: The certificate under Rule 4 is obtained from the auditor before the appointment is made and covers eligibility, compliance with statutory terms/limits, and pending proceedings, whereas the notice under section 139(1) (Form ADT-1) is filed by the company with the Registrar after the appointment, within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor was appointed
options.C: The certificate under Rule 4 is filed with the Registrar, while the notice under section 139(1) is retained internally by the company and never filed with any regulatory authority
options.D: The certificate under Rule 4 must be filed with NFRA in Form NFRA-1, while the notice under section 139(1) is addressed to the Central Government rather than the Registrar

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The certificate under Rule 4 is obtained from the auditor before the appointment is made and covers eligibility, compliance with statutory terms/limits, and pending proceedings, whereas the notice under section 139(1) (Form ADT-1) is filed by the company with the Registrar after the appointment, within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor was appointed

The Rule 4 certificate is an auditor-to-company document obtained before appointment (confirming eligibility, statutory compliance, and disclosure of pending proceedings), while the section 139(1) notice is a company-to-Registrar filing made after appointment, in Form ADT-1, within 15 days of the appointing meeting - the two serve different purposes and different recipients.

question_html: Section 139(2) applies to listed companies and certain other companies. What are those other companies, and what is the maximum term for which an individual and an audit firm respectively may be appointed or re-appointed as auditor of such companies?

options.A: Section 139(2) applies only to listed companies; all unlisted public and private companies are entirely outside its scope regardless of their paid-up capital, turnover, or public borrowings
options.B: The maximum term permitted is two terms of five consecutive years for an individual auditor and one term of five consecutive years for an audit firm - the reverse of the actual statutory allocation
options.C: Besides listed companies, section 139(2) applies to unlisted public companies with paid-up share capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, private companies with paid-up share capital of Rs. 50 crore or more, and companies (other than OPCs and small companies) with public borrowings from financial institutions, banks, or public deposits of Rs. 50 crore or more; such companies shall not appoint or re-appoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm for more than two terms of five consecutive years each
options.D: Section 139(2) applies to every company without exception (including one person companies and small companies), and permits an individual auditor to be appointed for unlimited consecutive terms so long as members re-elect him each year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Besides listed companies, section 139(2) applies to unlisted public companies with paid-up share capital of Rs. 10 crore or more, private companies with paid-up share capital of Rs. 50 crore or more, and companies (other than OPCs and small companies) with public borrowings from financial institutions, banks, or public deposits of Rs. 50 crore or more; such companies shall not appoint or re-appoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, or an audit firm for more than two terms of five consecutive years each

Section 139(2) extends the rotation requirement beyond listed companies to unlisted public companies with paid-up capital >= Rs. 10 crore, private companies with paid-up capital >= Rs. 50 crore, and companies (excluding OPCs/small companies) with public borrowings/deposits >= Rs. 50 crore, capping an individual auditor at one term of five consecutive years and an audit firm at two terms of five consecutive years each.

question_html: After completing the maximum permissible term(s), for how long is an individual auditor, and for how long is an audit firm, ineligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company?

options.A: Both an individual auditor and an audit firm become permanently and irrevocably barred from ever again being appointed as auditor of the same company, with no cooling-off period after which re-appointment becomes possible
options.B: The cooling period is three years for both an individual auditor and an audit firm, measured from the date of the AGM at which the auditor's term commenced rather than the date on which the term was completed
options.C: There is no cooling period at all under section 139(2); an individual or a firm may be immediately re-appointed as auditor of the same company the very next year after completing the maximum permissible term
options.D: An individual auditor who has completed one term of five consecutive years is not eligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of his term; an audit firm which has completed two terms of five consecutive years is not eligible for re-appointment in the same company for five years from the completion of its second term

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) An individual auditor who has completed one term of five consecutive years is not eligible for re-appointment as auditor in the same company for five years from the completion of his term; an audit firm which has completed two terms of five consecutive years is not eligible for re-appointment in the same company for five years from the completion of its second term

question_html: Does the rotation requirement under section 139(2) in any way restrict a company's right to remove an auditor, or an auditor's right to resign, before completion of the maximum permissible term?

options.A: No - the proviso to section 139(2) expressly states that nothing contained in the sub-section shall prejudice the right of the company to remove an auditor, or of the auditor to resign from office of the company, notwithstanding the rotation provisions
options.B: Yes - once an auditor is appointed under the rotation scheme, the company loses any right to remove that auditor before the full five-year (or ten-year, for a firm) term expires, and the auditor similarly loses the right to resign mid-term
options.C: The rotation provisions permit early removal of an auditor by the company, but expressly deny the auditor any corresponding right to resign before completing the mandated term
options.D: The rotation provisions permit an auditor to resign at will, but expressly deny the company any right to remove the auditor before the mandated term is completed, in order to preserve auditor independence

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - the proviso to section 139(2) expressly states that nothing contained in the sub-section shall prejudice the right of the company to remove an auditor, or of the auditor to resign from office of the company, notwithstanding the rotation provisions

The proviso to section 139(2) makes clear that the rotation scheme (maximum terms and cooling period) operates without prejudice to the company's separate statutory right to remove an auditor under section 140(1), or the auditor's right to resign under section 140(2) - rotation and removal/resignation are independent mechanisms.

question_html: Under Rule 6(3), is an incoming auditor eligible for appointment if it is associated with the outgoing auditor under the 'same network' of audit firms, and what happens if a partner who certified the company's financial statements retires from the outgoing firm and joins another firm?

options.A: The incoming auditor is always eligible for appointment regardless of any network association with the outgoing auditor, since Rule 6(3) applies only to individual auditors and not to audit firms operating under a common brand
options.B: The incoming auditor or audit firm is NOT eligible for appointment if it is associated with the outgoing auditor or audit firm under the same network (firms operating under the same brand name, trade name, or common control); further, if the partner in charge of the outgoing firm (who certified the financial statements) retires and joins another firm of chartered accountants, that other firm is also rendered ineligible for appointment for a cooling period of five years
options.C: Rule 6(3) disqualifies the incoming firm only if it shares the exact same legal name as the outgoing firm; firms merely operating under a common brand name, trade name, or common control (without an identical legal name) remain fully eligible
options.D: If a certifying partner of the outgoing firm retires and joins another firm, that other firm becomes immediately eligible to be appointed as the company's auditor with no restriction, since the cooling period applies only to the original outgoing firm and not to any firm the partner subsequently joins

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The incoming auditor or audit firm is NOT eligible for appointment if it is associated with the outgoing auditor or audit firm under the same network (firms operating under the same brand name, trade name, or common control); further, if the partner in charge of the outgoing firm (who certified the financial statements) retires and joins another firm of chartered accountants, that other firm is also rendered ineligible for appointment for a cooling period of five years

Rule 6(3) bars appointment of an incoming auditor/firm associated with the outgoing auditor/firm under the same network (common brand name, trade name, or control), and extends this ineligibility for five years to any other firm that a certifying common partner of the outgoing firm subsequently joins - closing an obvious route around the rotation requirement.

question_html: An individual has already functioned as auditor of a company for 4 consecutive years as at the point from which the section 139(2) rotation provisions must be complied with. As per the illustrative table for individual auditors, what is the maximum number of further consecutive years for which he may be appointed in the same company, and what aggregate period will he have completed?

options.A: Where 4 years have already been completed, the individual may be appointed for a further 5 consecutive years, giving an aggregate period of 9 years in the same company
options.B: Where 4 years have already been completed, the individual is immediately disqualified from any further appointment, and the aggregate period is capped strictly at the 4 years already served, with no further consecutive years thereafter permitted
options.C: Where 4 years have already been completed, the maximum further consecutive years for which the individual may be appointed is 3 years, giving an aggregate period of 7 years in the same company (before he must vacate under the transitional rotation scheme)
options.D: Where 4 years have already been completed, the individual may be appointed for a further 1 consecutive year only, giving an aggregate period of 5 years in the same company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Where 4 years have already been completed, the maximum further consecutive years for which the individual may be appointed is 3 years, giving an aggregate period of 7 years in the same company (before he must vacate under the transitional rotation scheme)

The illustrative transitional table for individual auditors provides that 4 years already completed permits a maximum of 3 further consecutive years, for an aggregate of 7 years in the same company - the aggregate period tapers as the pre-commencement tenure lengthens, ranging from 5 years (where 1 year had been served) up to 8 years or more (where 5 or more years had already been served).

options.A: The company is statutorily required to remove and replace all joint auditors simultaneously in the same year, regardless of when each joint auditor's individual term would otherwise expire
options.B: Rotation is inapplicable altogether where joint auditors are appointed, since Rule 6(4) exempts joint-auditor arrangements from the entire rotation scheme under section 139(2)

Rule 6(4) permits (rather than mandates) the company to stagger the rotation of joint auditors so that not all of them complete their respective terms in the same year - preserving continuity of institutional knowledge even as individual joint auditors rotate out over time.

question_html: Other than a Government company, who appoints the first auditor of a company, within what period, and until when does such auditor hold office?

options.A: The first auditor of a company (other than a Government company) shall be appointed by the Board of Directors within 30 days of the date of registration of the company, and the auditor so appointed shall hold office until the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting
options.B: The first auditor must be appointed by the members of the company in general meeting within 30 days of registration, and shall hold office for a fixed term of five consecutive years from such appointment
options.C: The first auditor must be appointed by the Managing Director acting alone within 60 days of registration, and shall hold office until the conclusion of the second Annual General Meeting
options.D: The first auditor must be appointed by the Registrar of Companies within 30 days of registration, and shall hold office until the Registrar directs otherwise

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The first auditor of a company (other than a Government company) shall be appointed by the Board of Directors within 30 days of the date of registration of the company, and the auditor so appointed shall hold office until the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting

Section 139(6) vests the power to appoint the first auditor (for companies other than Government companies) in the Board of Directors, to be exercised within 30 days of the date of registration; the first auditor so appointed holds office only until the conclusion of the first AGM - not for a fixed multi-year term.

question_html: If the Board of Directors fails to exercise its power to appoint the first auditor within the stipulated 30 days, what steps must follow, and until when does the resulting auditor hold office?

options.A: The company automatically has no auditor for that financial year, and the requirement to appoint a first auditor lapses permanently once the 30-day window has passed without Board action
options.B: The Board shall inform the members of the company, who shall appoint the first auditor within 90 days at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM); such auditor, however appointed, shall hold office till the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting
options.C: The Registrar of Companies is empowered to appoint the first auditor directly, without any requirement to inform the members or convene an extraordinary general meeting
options.D: The members must appoint the first auditor within 30 additional days (i.e., 60 days from registration in total) at the next scheduled AGM, since no separate EGM is contemplated by section 139(6)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The Board shall inform the members of the company, who shall appoint the first auditor within 90 days at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM); such auditor, however appointed, shall hold office till the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting

Where the Board fails to appoint the first auditor within 30 days of registration, section 139(6) requires it to inform the members, who must then appoint the first auditor within 90 days at an EGM; regardless of whether the Board or the members (at the EGM) make the appointment, the first auditor's tenure ends at the conclusion of the first AGM.

question_html: The Managing Director of a company, without consulting the Board, personally appoints a practicing Chartered Accountant as the company's first auditor. Is this appointment valid under section 139(6)?

options.A: Yes - since the Managing Director is the company's chief executive and de facto head of the Board, any appointment he personally makes on behalf of the company is automatically treated as a valid Board appointment under section 139(6)
options.B: Yes, provided the Managing Director ratifies his own appointment at the next Board meeting within 90 days, in which case the original appointment is deemed to have been valid retroactively from the date it was made
options.C: No - section 139(6) requires that the first auditor be appointed by the Board of Directors (as a collective body) within 30 days of the date of registration of the company; an appointment made unilaterally by the Managing Director without Board action violates section 139(6) and is invalid
options.D: The appointment is valid only if the auditor so appointed additionally obtains written approval from the Registrar of Companies within 15 days of the Managing Director's appointment letter

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No - section 139(6) requires that the first auditor be appointed by the Board of Directors (as a collective body) within 30 days of the date of registration of the company; an appointment made unilaterally by the Managing Director without Board action violates section 139(6) and is invalid

Section 139(6) squarely vests the power to appoint the first auditor in the Board of Directors as a body, not in any single director (even the Managing Director) acting alone; an appointment made without a Board resolution is therefore invalid for violating section 139(6).

question_html: The Government of a State holds 25% of the subscribed share capital of a company. Does this shareholding, by itself, make the company a 'Government company' so as to attract the CAG appointment provisions of section 139(5)/(7)?

options.A: Yes - any government shareholding whatsoever, however small, is sufficient by itself to classify a company as a 'Government company' and thereby attract the CAG appointment mechanism under section 139(5)/(7)
options.B: No - section 2(45) requires that not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital be held by the Central Government, or by one or more State Governments, or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, for a company to qualify as a 'Government company'; a 25% government shareholding alone does not meet this threshold, so the company remains a non-Government company for section 139 purposes
options.C: Yes - a 25% government shareholding exactly matches the statutory threshold of one-fourth prescribed under section 2(45) for classification as a 'Government company'
options.D: No such threshold exists under the Companies Act, 2013; whether a company is a 'Government company' is determined solely by whether any of its directors are government nominees, irrespective of shareholding

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - section 2(45) requires that not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital be held by the Central Government, or by one or more State Governments, or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, for a company to qualify as a 'Government company'; a 25% government shareholding alone does not meet this threshold, so the company remains a non-Government company for section 139 purposes

question_html: For a company whose accounts are NOT subject to audit by an auditor appointed by CAG, who fills a casual vacancy in the office of auditor, within what period, and what additional approval is required where the vacancy arises from the auditor's resignation?

options.A: Only the members in general meeting (never the Board) may fill any casual vacancy in the office of auditor, and no distinction is drawn between vacancies caused by resignation and those caused by any other reason
options.B: The Board may fill a casual vacancy within 90 days regardless of cause, and the auditor so appointed always holds office for a fresh five-year term rather than merely until the next AGM
options.C: The Board may fill any casual vacancy in the office of an auditor within 30 days, and any auditor so appointed holds office until the conclusion of the next AGM; however, where the vacancy is caused by the resignation of an auditor, such appointment by the Board must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the recommendation of the Board
options.D: Where the vacancy is caused by resignation, the Board's appointment requires approval of the Central Government (not a general meeting) within three months of the Board's recommendation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The Board may fill any casual vacancy in the office of an auditor within 30 days, and any auditor so appointed holds office until the conclusion of the next AGM; however, where the vacancy is caused by the resignation of an auditor, such appointment by the Board must also be approved by the company at a general meeting convened within three months of the recommendation of the Board

options.A: The casual vacancy shall be filled by the Central Government within 60 days, and if the Central Government fails to act, the vacancy remains unfilled until the next AGM with no further fallback mechanism
options.B: The casual vacancy shall always be filled by the members in general meeting within 30 days, with CAG having no role in filling casual vacancies for CAG-audited companies

options.D: The casual vacancy shall be filled by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India within 30 days; if CAG does not fill the vacancy within that period, the Board of Directors shall fill the vacancy within the next 30 days

question_html: Under section 139(9), what three conditions must be satisfied for a retiring auditor to be validly re-appointed at an AGM, and what does section 139(10) provide where no auditor is appointed or re-appointed at an AGM?

options.A: Under section 139(9), a retiring auditor may be re-appointed if: (a) he is not disqualified for re-appointment; (b) he has not given the company written notice of his unwillingness to be re-appointed; and (c) no special resolution has been passed at that meeting appointing some other auditor or expressly providing that he shall not be re-appointed; under section 139(10), where at any AGM no auditor is appointed or re-appointed, the existing auditor shall continue to be the auditor of the company (subject to the section 139(9) conditions being checked even in this deemed-continuation scenario)
options.B: The three conditions are: the auditor must be a Chartered Accountant, must hold a valid certificate of practice, and must not be a body corporate - none of which relate to disqualification, unwillingness, or a contrary special resolution
options.C: Section 139(10) provides that where no auditor is appointed or re-appointed at an AGM, the company is deemed to have no auditor at all until the next AGM, with the audit function suspended in the interim
options.D: The three section 139(9) conditions apply only to audit firms and not to individual auditors, since individual auditors are governed exclusively by section 139(6) regarding re-appointment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Under section 139(9), a retiring auditor may be re-appointed if: (a) he is not disqualified for re-appointment; (b) he has not given the company written notice of his unwillingness to be re-appointed; and (c) no special resolution has been passed at that meeting appointing some other auditor or expressly providing that he shall not be re-appointed; under section 139(10), where at any AGM no auditor is appointed or re-appointed, the existing auditor shall continue to be the auditor of the company (subject to the section 139(9) conditions being checked even in this deemed-continuation scenario)

Section 139(9) permits re-appointment of a retiring auditor only where he is not disqualified, has not expressed written unwillingness, and no special resolution excludes him; section 139(10)'s deeming provision (existing auditor continues if no appointment/re-appointment is made) still requires the section 139(9) conditions to be checked, per the express note in the study material.

question_html: AB Limited's General Meeting removed Mr. Suresh, the first auditor appointed by the Board, and appointed Mr. Gupta in his place, without seeking the approval of the Central Government. Is this removal valid?

options.A: Yes - since Mr. Suresh was only a first auditor (appointed by the Board rather than by the members), section 140(1)'s requirement of Central Government approval does not apply to his removal at all
options.B: Yes - a General Meeting resolution to remove any auditor, first or subsequent, automatically satisfies the requirements of section 140(1) without any need for separate Central Government approval
options.C: The removal is valid only for the remainder of the current financial year, after which Mr. Gupta must vacate and Mr. Suresh must be automatically reinstated as auditor
options.D: No - the removal is invalid; even a first auditor appointed by the Board can only be removed in accordance with section 140(1), which requires previous approval of the Central Government before a special resolution can validly effect the removal, so bypassing Central Government approval contravenes the Act

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - the removal is invalid; even a first auditor appointed by the Board can only be removed in accordance with section 140(1), which requires previous approval of the Central Government before a special resolution can validly effect the removal, so bypassing Central Government approval contravenes the Act

question_html: If an auditor resigns from a company, within what period must he file a statement, in what form, and with which authorities - distinguishing a Government company from other companies?

options.A: The auditor must file a statement in Form ADT-3 within 30 days from the date of resignation, indicating the reasons and other relevant facts; for other (non-Government) companies, the statement is filed with the company and the Registrar, whereas for a Government company (or one owned/controlled by Central/State Government(s)), it must additionally be filed with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India

question_html: What penalty applies to an auditor who fails to comply with the section 140(2) statement-filing requirement on resignation, including the position for continuing failure?

options.A: The auditor is liable to a flat penalty of Rs. 2 lakh with no lower threshold and no reference to the auditor's remuneration, and no additional daily penalty applies for continuing failure
options.B: The auditor is liable to a penalty of Rs. 50,000 or an amount equal to the remuneration of the auditor, whichever is less; in case of continuing failure, a further penalty of Rs. 500 for each day after the first during which the failure continues, subject to a maximum of Rs. 2 lakh
options.C: The auditor is liable to a penalty of Rs. 5 lakh or an amount equal to four times his remuneration, whichever is lower, mirroring the penalty structure applicable to contraventions of sections 139, 144, or 145
options.D: The auditor is liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, with no monetary fine at all, for failing to file the resignation statement within 30 days

question_html: Which of the following correctly summarizes the recipients of the ADT-3 resignation statement, contrasting a Government company with other companies?

question_html: When is special notice required for a resolution at an AGM appointing a person other than a retiring auditor (or providing that a retiring auditor shall not be re-appointed), and what must the company do upon receiving notice of such a resolution?

options.A: Special notice is required in every case of appointing an auditor other than the retiring auditor, regardless of how long the retiring auditor has already served, and the company has no obligation to inform the retiring auditor of such a resolution
options.B: Special notice is required only where the retiring auditor has already completed his full permissible tenure (five years for an individual, ten years for a firm), i.e., the opposite of the actual statutory trigger
options.C: Special notice is required only if the retiring auditor is a firm and never if the retiring auditor is an individual, and the company need only inform the Registrar (not the retiring auditor) of such a resolution
options.D: Special notice is required where the retiring auditor has not completed a consecutive tenure of five years (or ten years, in the case of a firm, as applicable); on receiving notice of such a resolution, the company shall forthwith send a copy thereof to the retiring auditor

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Special notice is required where the retiring auditor has not completed a consecutive tenure of five years (or ten years, in the case of a firm, as applicable); on receiving notice of such a resolution, the company shall forthwith send a copy thereof to the retiring auditor

Section 140(4) requires special notice for a resolution appointing someone other than the retiring auditor (or excluding his re-appointment) specifically where that auditor has NOT yet completed his consecutive tenure of five years (individual) or ten years (firm); on such notice, the company must forthwith forward a copy to the retiring auditor, who then has representation rights.

question_html: On what three alternative bases may the Tribunal (NCLT) act to order a company to change its auditors under section 140(5), and what are the consequences for an auditor against whom a final order is passed?

options.A: The Tribunal may act (a) suo motu (on its own), (b) on an application made to it by the Central Government (Form NCLT-9), or (c) on an application made to it by any person concerned (Form NCLT-9), where satisfied that the auditor has, directly or indirectly, acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud in relation to the company or its directors/officers; an auditor against whom a final order is passed is not eligible to be appointed as auditor of any company for 5 years from the date of the order, and is also liable for action under section 447
options.B: The Tribunal may act only on an application by the Central Government; it has no suo motu power and cannot act on an application made by any other concerned person under section 140(5)
options.C: The consequence of a final order is a permanent, lifetime ban on the auditor from being appointed as auditor of any company, with no fixed five-year period, and no additional liability under section 447
options.D: The Tribunal's power under section 140(5) is limited to issuing a warning to the auditor; it cannot direct the company to actually change its auditor under any circumstance

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The Tribunal may act (a) suo motu (on its own), (b) on an application made to it by the Central Government (Form NCLT-9), or (c) on an application made to it by any person concerned (Form NCLT-9), where satisfied that the auditor has, directly or indirectly, acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud in relation to the company or its directors/officers; an auditor against whom a final order is passed is not eligible to be appointed as auditor of any company for 5 years from the date of the order, and is also liable for action under section 447

Section 140(5) gives the Tribunal three routes to act (suo motu, on CG application, or on application by any concerned person) where satisfied of fraud, abetment, or collusion by the auditor; a final adverse order carries a 5-year appointment ineligibility (not a lifetime ban) plus separate liability under section 447 - and where a firm is involved, liability attaches to the firm and to every partner who acted fraudulently, abetted, or colluded.

question_html: If a copy of the retiring auditor's written representation is not sent to members (either because it was received too late or due to the company's default), what recourse does the auditor have, and what safeguard exists against abuse of this representation right?

options.A: The auditor has no recourse whatsoever if the representation copy is not sent to members; the right lapses entirely and cannot be revived by requiring it to be read out at the meeting
options.B: The auditor may (without prejudice to his right to be heard orally) require that the representation be read out at the meeting, and a copy of such representation shall be filed with the Registrar; separately, if the Tribunal is satisfied on an application (Form NCLT-1) that these rights are being abused by the auditor, it may order that the representation need not be sent and need not be read out at the meeting
options.C: The auditor may require the representation to be read out at the meeting, but no copy need ever be filed with the Registrar under any circumstance, and the Tribunal has no power to curtail this right even in cases of abuse
options.D: The safeguard against abuse operates automatically without any Tribunal application - the company itself may unilaterally decide, without judicial oversight, that the representation right is being abused and refuse to read it out

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The auditor may (without prejudice to his right to be heard orally) require that the representation be read out at the meeting, and a copy of such representation shall be filed with the Registrar; separately, if the Tribunal is satisfied on an application (Form NCLT-1) that these rights are being abused by the auditor, it may order that the representation need not be sent and need not be read out at the meeting

Where a representation copy is not sent to members (whether due to lateness or company default), the auditor may require it be read out at the meeting and a copy be filed with the Registrar; the second proviso to section 140(4), read with Rule 78 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, allows the Tribunal - on an application in Form NCLT-1 - to dispense with both safeguards where it is satisfied the auditor is abusing these rights.

question_html: Section 141(1) defines an eligible auditor by cross-reference to another statute. Which statute, and which specific provisions of it, are referenced for the meaning of 'Chartered Accountant' and 'certificate of practice'?

options.A: The Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - specifically section 2(1)(b) for the definition of 'Chartered Accountant', and section 6(1) for the requirement of holding a valid certificate of practice
options.B: The Companies Act, 2013 itself, specifically sections 2(1)(b) and 6(1) of that very Act, without any cross-reference to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 at all
options.C: The Cost and Works Accountants Act, 1959, since section 141(1) treats Chartered Accountants and Cost Accountants as interchangeable for purposes of statutory audit eligibility
options.D: The Company Secretaries Act, 1980, on the basis that company secretaries in practice are equally eligible for appointment as statutory auditors under section 141(1)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 - specifically section 2(1)(b) for the definition of 'Chartered Accountant', and section 6(1) for the requirement of holding a valid certificate of practice

question_html: Which of the following persons are disqualified from being appointed as auditor of a company under section 141(3)(a) to (c)?

options.A: Only natural persons who are direct employees of the company are disqualified; body corporates (including ordinary companies) and LLPs are both fully eligible for appointment as auditor under section 141(3)
options.B: (a) A body corporate, other than an LLP registered under the LLP Act, 2008; (b) an officer or employee of the company; and (c) a person who is a partner, or who is in the employment, of an officer or employee of the company
options.C: A body corporate is disqualified only if it is registered as an LLP under the LLP Act, 2008; ordinary (non-LLP) body corporates remain eligible for appointment as auditor
options.D: A person who is a partner of an officer or employee of the company is eligible for appointment, so long as he himself holds no direct employment relationship with the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) (a) A body corporate, other than an LLP registered under the LLP Act, 2008; (b) an officer or employee of the company; and (c) a person who is a partner, or who is in the employment, of an officer or employee of the company

question_html: Under section 141(3)(d)(i), is a person disqualified from appointment as auditor if he himself holds any security or interest in the company, however small? What threshold applies where it is instead a RELATIVE of the auditor who holds such security or interest, and within what period must corrective action be taken if that relative's threshold is breached?

options.A: A person is disqualified only if his holding of securities exceeds Rs. 1,00,000 in face value; holdings below that threshold, whether by the auditor himself or by his relative, are permitted without any disqualification
options.B: There is no threshold distinction between the auditor himself and his relative - both are permitted to hold securities or interest in the company up to Rs. 5,00,000 in face value without any disqualification arising
options.C: Yes - if the auditor himself, or his partner, holds any security of or interest in the company (or its subsidiary, holding, associate, or fellow subsidiary company), he is disqualified regardless of the amount; the proviso permits a RELATIVE of the auditor to hold such security or interest up to a face value of Rs. 1,00,000, and corrective action to restore compliance must be taken by the auditor within 60 days of the relative's acquisition of security or interest beyond that threshold
options.D: Corrective action for a relative's threshold breach must be taken within 30 days (not 60 days) of the acquisition, failing which the disqualification becomes permanent and cannot be cured

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - if the auditor himself, or his partner, holds any security of or interest in the company (or its subsidiary, holding, associate, or fellow subsidiary company), he is disqualified regardless of the amount; the proviso permits a RELATIVE of the auditor to hold such security or interest up to a face value of Rs. 1,00,000, and corrective action to restore compliance must be taken by the auditor within 60 days of the relative's acquisition of security or interest beyond that threshold

The rule is asymmetric: the auditor himself (or his partner) is disqualified by holding ANY security or interest, however small, whereas the Rs. 1,00,000 face-value threshold is a proviso benefit available only to a RELATIVE of the auditor; if that relative's holding crosses the threshold, the auditor has 60 days from the acquisition to take corrective action to restore compliance.

options.A: The indebtedness threshold is Rs. 1 lakh and the guarantee/security threshold is Rs. 5 lakh - the reverse of the actual statutory allocation between the two clauses
options.B: Both the indebtedness threshold and the guarantee/security threshold are set at Rs. 10 lakh, with no distinction drawn between direct indebtedness and third-party guarantees
options.C: There is no monetary threshold for either indebtedness or guarantee/security; any indebtedness or guarantee of any amount whatsoever, however small, results in disqualification under section 141(3)(d)
options.D: A person is disqualified if he, his relative, or his partner is indebted to the company (or its subsidiary/holding/associate company or fellow subsidiary) in excess of Rs. 5 lakh; separately, a person is disqualified if he, his relative, or his partner has given a guarantee or provided security in connection with the indebtedness of a third person to the company (or such related companies) in excess of Rs. 1 lakh

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A person is disqualified if he, his relative, or his partner is indebted to the company (or its subsidiary/holding/associate company or fellow subsidiary) in excess of Rs. 5 lakh; separately, a person is disqualified if he, his relative, or his partner has given a guarantee or provided security in connection with the indebtedness of a third person to the company (or such related companies) in excess of Rs. 1 lakh

Section 141(3)(d)(ii) sets the indebtedness disqualification threshold at Rs. 5 lakh, while section 141(3)(d)(iii) sets a lower threshold of Rs. 1 lakh for guarantees or security given in connection with a third person's indebtedness to the company - two distinct clauses with two distinct monetary limits.

question_html: Section 141(3)(e) disqualifies a person or firm having a 'business relationship' with the company (or related companies). What does 'business relationship' mean, and what two categories of transaction are expressly excluded from this meaning?

options.A: 'Business relationship' means any transaction entered into for a commercial purpose, EXCEPT: (i) commercial transactions in the nature of professional services permitted to be rendered by an auditor or audit firm under the Companies Act and the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (and rules/regulations thereunder); and (ii) commercial transactions in the ordinary course of business of the company at arm's length price, such as purchase of products or services from companies like telecommunications, airlines, hospitals, hotels, and similar businesses, where the auditor is merely a customer
options.B: 'Business relationship' covers only relationships arising from a written contract; purely oral or informal commercial arrangements between the auditor and the company are entirely outside the scope of section 141(3)(e), whatever their scale
options.C: The only exception to 'business relationship' is where the transaction value is below Rs. 1 lakh; both professional-service transactions and arm's-length ordinary-course transactions are treated as disqualifying regardless of value
options.D: 'Business relationship' is disqualifying only if the auditor is the SELLER (not the buyer/customer) in the transaction; arm's-length purchases by the auditor as a customer are disqualifying but purchases by the company from the auditor are not

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) 'Business relationship' means any transaction entered into for a commercial purpose, EXCEPT: (i) commercial transactions in the nature of professional services permitted to be rendered by an auditor or audit firm under the Companies Act and the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (and rules/regulations thereunder); and (ii) commercial transactions in the ordinary course of business of the company at arm's length price, such as purchase of products or services from companies like telecommunications, airlines, hospitals, hotels, and similar businesses, where the auditor is merely a customer

Section 141(3)(e) casts a wide net over commercial-purpose transactions but expressly excludes permitted professional services and arm's-length ordinary-course transactions (e.g., the auditor buying air tickets, hotel rooms, or telecom/hospital services from the company as an ordinary customer) - preserving the practical reality that an auditor may transact with a client company as any other customer would.

question_html: Under section 141(3)(g), what is the maximum number of companies of which a person (or, in the case of a firm, EACH partner) may hold audit appointments, and which categories of company are excluded when computing this ceiling?

options.A: The ceiling is 20 companies per FIRM (not per individual partner); so a firm with five CA partners is still capped at a firm-wide total of 20 company audits regardless of how many partners it has
options.B: A person (in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person/partner of a firm holding auditor appointments) is disqualified if, at the date of appointment or re-appointment, he already holds appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies; while computing this ceiling, one person companies, dormant companies, small companies, and private companies having paid-up share capital less than Rs. 100 crore are excluded (the private-company exclusion being available only where such companies have not defaulted in filing financial statements under section 137 or annual returns under section 92)
options.C: The ceiling applies uniformly to every company without exception, including one person companies, dormant companies, small companies, and all private companies, with no carve-outs of any kind
options.D: The ceiling is 50 companies (not 20), reflecting the higher threshold applicable to large audit firms with multiple Chartered Accountant partners

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) A person (in full-time employment elsewhere, or a person/partner of a firm holding auditor appointments) is disqualified if, at the date of appointment or re-appointment, he already holds appointment as auditor of more than 20 companies; while computing this ceiling, one person companies, dormant companies, small companies, and private companies having paid-up share capital less than Rs. 100 crore are excluded (the private-company exclusion being available only where such companies have not defaulted in filing financial statements under section 137 or annual returns under section 92)

The 20-company ceiling under section 141(3)(g) operates PER PERSON - so a firm with 3 partners is collectively eligible for 3 x 20 = 60 company audits (illustrated in the study material with ABC & Co., whose partners already held 4, 6, and 10 audits respectively, leaving 40 further audits available to the firm); OPCs, dormant companies, small companies, and qualifying private companies (paid-up capital < Rs. 100 crore, not in default of S.137/S.92 filings) are excluded from the count.

question_html: Under section 141(3)(h), for how long after a conviction involving fraud is a person disqualified from appointment as auditor, and what happens under section 141(4) if a person incurs any section 141(3) disqualification AFTER his appointment as auditor?

options.A: The fraud-conviction disqualification lasts for 5 years (not 10) from the date of conviction, and post-appointment disqualification under section 141(4) requires a formal removal resolution before the auditor is treated as having vacated office
options.B: The fraud-conviction disqualification is permanent and lifelong with no expiry, and section 141(4) provides that post-appointment disqualification has no legal consequence unless and until the company passes a special resolution to remove the auditor
options.C: A person convicted by a court of an offence involving fraud is disqualified from appointment as auditor for a period of 10 years from the date of such conviction (i.e., disqualification applies as long as 10 years have not elapsed since conviction); under section 141(4), if an auditor incurs any section 141(3) disqualification after his appointment, he shall be deemed to have vacated his office as auditor, and such vacation is deemed to be a casual vacancy

question_html: Under section 143(1), what right of access does every auditor have to the company's books of account and vouchers, what is he entitled to require from officers, and what additional access does the auditor of a HOLDING company have with respect to subsidiaries and associates?

options.A: Every auditor has a right of access AT ALL TIMES to the books of account and vouchers of the company, whether kept at the registered office or at any other place; he is entitled to require from officers such information and explanations as he considers necessary for performance of his duties; and the auditor of a holding company additionally has the right of access to the records of all its subsidiaries and associate companies, in so far as such access relates to consolidation of financial statements
options.B: The auditor's right of access to books and vouchers is limited to normal business hours at the registered office only; access to books kept at any other location requires prior written permission from the Board of Directors
options.C: The auditor is entitled to require information and explanations only from the Managing Director personally, and not from any other officer of the company, however senior
options.D: The holding company's auditor has NO right of access to subsidiary or associate company records under any circumstance; each subsidiary's own auditor must independently furnish all consolidation-related information

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Every auditor has a right of access AT ALL TIMES to the books of account and vouchers of the company, whether kept at the registered office or at any other place; he is entitled to require from officers such information and explanations as he considers necessary for performance of his duties; and the auditor of a holding company additionally has the right of access to the records of all its subsidiaries and associate companies, in so far as such access relates to consolidation of financial statements

Section 143(1) grants an expansive 'at all times' access right to books/vouchers wherever kept, a broad entitlement to require information/explanations from officers, and - critically for group reporting - extends the holding company auditor's access rights to subsidiary and associate company records to the extent necessary for consolidation of financial statements.

question_html: SHRD Private Ltd. proposed appointment of its statutory auditors at a Board meeting, but the remuneration was not finalized at that time; the engagement letter was signed with a clause stating the fee would be mutually decided later. Is this arrangement valid?

options.A: No - section 142 mandates that remuneration must be finally fixed and stated in the engagement letter itself at the time of signing, failing which the entire appointment of the auditor becomes void ab initio
options.B: Yes - such an arrangement is valid; section 142 does not require the remuneration to be finalized at the moment of appointment or engagement-letter signing, so an engagement letter with a 'fee to be mutually decided' clause does not violate the Companies Act, 2013

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - such an arrangement is valid; section 142 does not require the remuneration to be finalized at the moment of appointment or engagement-letter signing, so an engagement letter with a 'fee to be mutually decided' clause does not violate the Companies Act, 2013

The study material's own example confirms that an engagement letter leaving the fee to be 'mutually decided' later is a valid arrangement - section 142 governs how and by whom remuneration is fixed (general meeting/Board), but does not require that figure to be locked in before the engagement letter is executed.

Under section 147(1), what is the minimum and maximum fine to which Vantage Industries Limited (the company) is liable, and what is the minimum and maximum fine to which the officer of the company who is in default is liable, for the contravention of section 139?

options.D: Contravention of section 139 attracts imprisonment (not a fine) for both the company and the officer in default, for a term which may extend to one year

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The company is punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 25,000, which may extend to Rs. 5,00,000; every officer of the company who is in default is punishable with a fine of not less than Rs. 10,000, which may extend to Rs. 1,00,000

Section 147(1) fixes the company's fine at Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 5,00,000, and the fine for every officer of the company in default at the lower range of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 1,00,000, for contravention of any of sections 139 to 146.

Since Mr. Oberoi knowingly and willfully contravened section 139 with the intention to deceive the shareholders, what enhanced penalty does he face under the proviso to section 147(2), beyond the ordinary penalty applicable to auditors?

options.A: He faces only the ordinary auditor penalty of a fine not less than Rs. 25,000 extending to Rs. 5,00,000 or four times his remuneration (whichever is less), with no enhancement and no imprisonment for willful, deceptive contravention
options.B: He faces imprisonment for a term which may extend to 5 years, with no fine component at all, since the proviso to section 147(2) replaces the fine entirely with imprisonment for willful contravention
options.C: He shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 1 year, and with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 50,000 but which may extend to Rs. 25,00,000 or eight times his remuneration, whichever is less
options.D: He faces a fine of exactly Rs. 25,00,000 with no variation and no imprisonment component, since the proviso to section 147(2) prescribes a flat fixed penalty rather than a range

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) He shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to 1 year, and with a fine which shall not be less than Rs. 50,000 but which may extend to Rs. 25,00,000 or eight times his remuneration, whichever is less

The proviso to section 147(2) enhances the auditor's ordinary penalty where the contravention of section 139, 144, or 145 was knowing or willful with intent to deceive - imprisonment up to 1 year plus a fine of the lower of Rs. 25,00,000 or eight times the auditor's remuneration (subject to the Rs. 50,000 floor), materially harsher than the ordinary fine-only penalty under section 147(2).

Can Vantage Industries Limited validly appoint Mr. Oberoi, its existing statutory auditor appointed under section 139, as the Cost Accountant to conduct the cost audit under section 148?

options.A: Yes - there is no restriction under the Companies Act, 2013 on the same person acting as both the statutory auditor under section 139 and the cost auditor under section 148 of the same company
options.B: Yes, provided Mr. Oberoi obtains prior written approval of the Audit Committee before accepting the cost audit engagement, since Committee approval overrides the proviso to section 148(3)
options.C: The restriction applies only where the statutory auditor is a firm; since Mr. Oberoi is appointed in his individual capacity as statutory auditor, the proviso to section 148(3) does not apply to him
options.D: No - the proviso to section 148(3) expressly provides that no person (or firm, including an LLP) appointed under section 139 as an auditor of the company shall be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, or vice versa; since Mr. Oberoi is already Vantage Industries Limited's statutory auditor under section 139, he cannot also be appointed as its cost auditor

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) No - the proviso to section 148(3) expressly provides that no person (or firm, including an LLP) appointed under section 139 as an auditor of the company shall be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, or vice versa; since Mr. Oberoi is already Vantage Industries Limited's statutory auditor under section 139, he cannot also be appointed as its cost auditor

The proviso to section 148(3) creates a strict mutual exclusivity between the statutory audit under section 139 and the cost audit under section 148 - the same person or firm cannot hold both appointments for the same company, so Mr. Oberoi is ineligible to be appointed as Vantage Industries Limited's cost auditor while he remains its section 139 statutory auditor.
